segments.name: What's the Go o' That: Glenlair and the Edinburgh Schoolrooms

stops.name: 14 India Street, Edinburgh, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 June 1831; older reference works print a November date, and the modern consensus followed here is June
stops.campa: John Clerk Maxwell, advocate, and Frances Cay have a son in the New Town house at 14 India Street. The father is a laird more interested in machinery than in law, given to inspecting drainage works and carts and any contrivance that moves; the mother is nearly forty and will teach the boy herself. The surname Maxwell comes from the Middlebie land in Galloway the family has inherited. Within two years the household leaves this address for that land, and keeps Edinburgh afterwards only as a winter lodging in other people's houses.
suggested_refs: 14 India Street, Edinburgh, the birth house, later acquired by the James Clerk Maxwell Foundation
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Glenlair, the estate and the question
stops.date_confidence: the family's relocation is attested to 1833; the month and day are set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: His father builds a new house on the Middlebie land and calls it Glenlair. The boy grows up among ditchers, masons and the working of a small estate, and he asks about all of it, relentlessly, until an answer holds. He catches sunlight on a tin plate and runs the disc of it round a darkened room, and when his father asks what he is about he answers that it is the sun and that he got it in with the tin plate. In April 1834 his father writes to Jane Cay that Master James is in great go. He is two years and ten months old.
stops.quote: What's the go o' that? What does it do?
stops.quote_source: Maxwell's cousin Jemima Blackburn, recalling his constant childhood question, in Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.28
suggested_refs: John Clerk Maxwell to Jane Cay, Corsock, 25 April 1834, printed in Campbell and Garnett (1882), p.27
sources: James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), pp.27-31
Wikipedia, 'Glenlair House'

stops.name: Glenlair, the death of Frances Cay
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1839; the day is set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: Frances Cay dies of abdominal cancer at Glenlair. She had taught her son his letters and heard his lessons herself, holding the whole of his education in her own hands; he is eight years old. The boy stays on the estate with his father through the winter that follows, and within two years the family sends him to Edinburgh for school and lodges him with his aunt through the terms. Forty years on, the same disease will kill him in the same part of the body. What he said at the time is not preserved in any letter that survives.
suggested_refs: Campbell and Garnett's account of the Glenlair household after 1839
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell

stops.name: Edinburgh Academy, the boy they call Dafty
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1841; the day is set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: He arrives in November into a class already formed, lodging through the terms at his aunt Isabella Wedderburn's house in Heriot Row. He wears clothes his father designed himself, speaks broad Galloway, and answers questions sideways. The class names him Dafty, and the name sticks for years. Two boys in it do not join the naming: Lewis Campbell, who will write his life, and Peter Guthrie Tait, who will argue physics with him by post for thirty years. He does not complain about it to anyone. He begins taking the class prizes in mathematics.
suggested_refs: 31 Heriot Row, Edinburgh, the Wedderburn house where Maxwell lodged in term time
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Wikipedia, 'Heriot Row'

stops.name: Glenlair, the ovals drawn with pins and string
stops.date_confidence: the work is attested to 1846, when Maxwell was fourteen; the month and day are set to 01 as unknown, and Glenlair is given as the pin though the sources place the work loosely between Glenlair and Edinburgh
stops.campa: At fourteen he works out how to draw an oval with pins, string and a pencil, generalizing the gardener's two-focus ellipse to curves with three foci and more, each focus weighted by a whole number of turns of the loop. He does not know that Descartes had studied the same curves two centuries earlier. He arrives at them from the string. His father shows the work to James David Forbes, professor of natural philosophy at the university, who reads it, checks it against Descartes, and reports that the boy's method is the simpler of the two.
suggested_refs: Maxwell, 'On the Description of Oval Curves, and Those Having a Plurality of Foci', Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh (1846)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org

stops.name: The Mound, Forbes reads the paper to the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: attested to 6 April 1846
stops.campa: On the sixth of April the paper On the Description of Oval Curves, and Those Having a Plurality of Foci is read to the Royal Society of Edinburgh, which meets in the Royal Institution building on the Mound. Forbes reads it aloud, because the author is fourteen and a schoolboy and cannot present his own work to the Society. Maxwell sits in the room and listens to his own sentences in another man's voice. The Society prints the paper in its Proceedings for the session. Some ninety more will follow over the next thirty-three years.
stops.quote: This work was remarkable for a 14 year old.
stops.quote_source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
suggested_refs: The Royal Institution building on the Mound, Edinburgh, meeting place of the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1846
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell

stops.name: University of Edinburgh, Old College, the three professors
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1847; the day is set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: At sixteen he enters the university: mathematics from Philip Kelland, natural philosophy from Forbes, logic and metaphysics from Sir William Hamilton the metaphysician, who is no relation to William Rowan Hamilton of Dublin, whose quaternions will occupy him later. He finds the lectures leave him time and spends it at Glenlair, building apparatus for polarized light out of glass, gelatin and whatever the estate yields, photographing the coloured stress patterns inside bent jelly. Three papers reach the Royal Society of Edinburgh before he leaves for England.
suggested_refs: Maxwell's early papers on rolling curves and on the equilibrium of elastic solids, Royal Society of Edinburgh, 1848-1850
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

segments.name: Cambridge: The Wranglers and Faraday's Lines

stops.name: Peterhouse, Cambridge, the first term
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1850; the day is set to 01 as unknown. The pin is the Peterhouse coordinate already carried in lord_kelvin.journey.json
stops.campa: He leaves Scotland at nineteen and matriculates at Peterhouse, the oldest and smallest of the colleges, where William Thomson had matriculated nine years before him. The two will correct each other's physics by letter for thirty years and never share a college, because Maxwell stays here less than a term. Peterhouse is thick with mathematicians and thin on fellowships, and a Scot with no connections can do that arithmetic. His father agrees to the move, and he crosses to Trinity before the term is out.
suggested_refs: Peterhouse admissions register, Michaelmas term 1850
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge, Hopkins and the Apostles
stops.date_confidence: the transfer to Trinity is attested to Maxwell's first Cambridge term, late 1850; this date is set to the start of 1851 to order the coaching years that follow. The pin is the Trinity College coordinate already carried in newton.journey.json
stops.campa: He reads for the Tripos under William Hopkins, the private coach whose pupils take the top places year after year, and joins the Apostles, the club where a dozen undergraduates read each other essays on whatever will not fit inside a lecture: analogy, evidence, whether mind can know matter at all. The training is brutal and narrow and he submits to it entirely. He is in Newton's college, two centuries after Newton took his own degree in the same courts, and the syllabus Hopkins drills him on is still built out of what Newton left behind.
suggested_refs: The Cambridge Apostles minute books for the early 1850s
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Otley, Suffolk, the illness at the rectory
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1853; the parish is Otley, where Charles Benjamin Tayler was rector from 1846, and the month and day are an estimate within that summer. The coordinate is Otley village and has not been checked against a gazetteer
stops.campa: In the summer he stays with the Reverend Charles Benjamin Tayler at Otley, brought there by Tayler's nephew, a Trinity undergraduate he is friendly with, and falls seriously ill in the house. The Taylers nurse him through it. What comes out of the sickroom is not only a recovery: his letters afterwards carry a hardened evangelical commitment that never leaves him, and that will sit beside the physics for the rest of his life without either being asked to answer for the other. He is twenty-two.
suggested_refs: Maxwell's letters of 1853-1854 on his religious commitment, printed in Campbell and Garnett (1882)
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Wikipedia, 'Charles Benjamin Tayler'

stops.name: Senate House, Cambridge, Second Wrangler
stops.date_confidence: the Tripos result is attested to January 1854; the day is set to 01 as unknown. The pin is the Senate House coordinate already carried in lord_kelvin.journey.json
stops.campa: After days of written examination in the Senate House he is placed Second Wrangler, behind Edward Routh. In the Smith's Prize examination, set on deeper ground by different examiners, the two are bracketed equal and neither is put above the other. Thomson had been Second Wrangler nine years earlier and had taken the Smith's Prize outright. Routh will spend his working life coaching other men through the same examination and publish no physics of his own. Maxwell takes his degree and stays on in Cambridge.
stops.quote: he obtained the position of Second Wrangler, and was bracketed equal with the Senior Wrangler
stops.quote_source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
suggested_refs: The Mathematical Tripos order of merit, January 1854, Senate House, Cambridge
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge, elected Fellow
stops.date_confidence: attested to 10 October 1855
stops.campa: Trinity elects him a Fellow. He is twenty-four, with a college income, rooms and no obligation but to think, and he spends the freedom on two things at once. Electricity he decides to learn from Michael Faraday rather than from the mathematicians, and Faraday's Experimental Researches contains no equations at all; he reads the whole of it before he opens anyone's mathematical treatment. Colour he takes up with painted tops, spinning them until the eye can no longer see anything but grey, then reading the sector widths off as numbers.
suggested_refs: Michael Faraday, Experimental Researches in Electricity, read entire by Maxwell before he took up the subject mathematically
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell

stops.name: Cambridge Philosophical Society, On Faraday's Lines of Force
stops.date_confidence: read in two parts, one in 1855 and one in 1856; the date given is the first reading, with month and day estimated. Chronologies that date the whole paper to 1855 silently drop the second part
stops.campa: He reads the paper in two sittings, months apart, before a room of Cambridge mathematicians. What he does in it is translation. Faraday's lines and tubes of force, drawn by a bookbinder's apprentice who could not do the calculus, become the streamlines of an incompressible fluid moving through space, and Faraday's spatial intuitions turn out to have equations waiting for them. He sends the paper to Faraday, who is sixty-four and has never been told his lines were mathematics, and to William Thomson, whose fluid analogies he has been reading since 1854.
stops.quote: In order to obtain physical ideas without adopting a physical theory we must make ourselves familiar with the existence of physical analogies.
stops.quote_source: James Clerk Maxwell, On Faraday's Lines of Force (1855-56), opening section, Wikisource transcription
suggested_refs: Maxwell to Faraday, on sending him On Faraday's Lines of Force; Cambridge University Library digitized Faraday correspondence
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Wikisource, 'On Faraday's Lines of Force'

stops.name: Glenlair, the death of John Clerk Maxwell
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 April 1856
stops.campa: His father dies at Glenlair in the spring. Maxwell has applied for the natural philosophy chair at Marischal College in Aberdeen partly to be within reach of the estate and the old man, and the appointment is confirmed after the death. John Clerk Maxwell is buried in the kirkyard at Parton, a few miles from the house he built. His son is twenty-four, laird of Glenlair as well as Fellow of Trinity, answerable for tenants, drains and roofs in Galloway while lecturing on the other side of Scotland. He keeps both for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Glenlair estate papers of the Clerk Maxwell family
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'Glenlair House'

stops.name: Marischal College, Aberdeen, the chair at twenty-five
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1856; the day is set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: He takes up the professorship of natural philosophy at twenty-five, younger than most of his students' fathers, and writes his own curriculum for it. The teaching runs some fifteen hours a week and he adds to that, unpaid, an evening class for the working men of the town, tradesmen and mechanics who come after their shifts. Aberdeen finds him remote and complains that his lectures go over the heads of the class. He is not much interested in the complaint. In the same rooms he starts calculating the rings of Saturn.
suggested_refs: Marischal College, Aberdeen, natural philosophy class records, 1856-1860
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Marischal College, the rings of Saturn
stops.date_confidence: the Adams Prize was awarded in 1857 per MacTutor, the Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology and the Adams Prize winners list; Wikipedia's Maxwell article gives 1859, which is the year the essay was published as a monograph. The contradiction is left standing. Month and day set to 01
stops.campa: The Adams Prize asks whether the rings of Saturn can be solid, fluid, or something else. Maxwell spends two years on the question and answers it: a solid ring would be torn apart by its own rotation, a fluid ring would break up into blobs by wave instability, and the only arrangement that survives is a swarm of separate bodies, uncountably many, each on its own orbit, held into a sheet by gravity and by nothing else. He wins the prize in 1857 and publishes the essay as a monograph two years later.
suggested_refs: Maxwell, On the Stability of the Motion of Saturn's Rings (Macmillan, 1859), the Adams Prize essay
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Wikipedia, 'Adams Prize'

stops.name: Old Machar, Aberdeen, the marriage to Katherine Dewar
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia and the Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology both give 2 June 1858; MacTutor gives June 1859. The discrepancy is not resolved here
stops.campa: He becomes engaged in February to Katherine Mary Dewar, daughter of the principal of his own college, and they marry in the Old Machar parish in June. She is about seven years older than he is. There will be no children. Colleagues find her difficult company; he does not. She takes readings for his experiments on the viscosity of gases, holding thermometers steady in a room heated past anything comfortable while he works the other end of the apparatus. She will nurse him through the smallpox and the erysipelas, and through the illness that kills him.
suggested_refs: St Machar's Cathedral, The Chanonry, Old Aberdeen, the Old Machar parish church
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell

stops.name: Marischal College, the colour top and the free class
stops.date_confidence: the Aberdeen colour work runs across the Marischal years and is not tied to a single date; 1859 is set to order the segment, and the month and day are set to 01
stops.campa: He spins discs of coloured paper on a top until the eye can no longer tell the mixture from a reference grey, then reads the sector widths off as numbers. Out of that comes an account of colour as three measurable quantities, and a diagnosis of colour blindness as a shortfall in one of the eye's three responses rather than a fault in its optics. A condition described for two generations now has a number attached to it. He tests his own students with the spinning top and writes down what each of them reports seeing.
suggested_refs: Maxwell's colour top and the colour box, instruments now held by the James Clerk Maxwell Foundation
sources: James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

segments.name: London: The Field Becomes a Theory

stops.name: Burlington House, the theory of compound colours
stops.date_confidence: the paper is attested to 1860 and the Rumford Medal followed; the month and day are set to 01 as unknown. The venue is Burlington House, the Royal Society's premises from 1857, not Somerset House, which the Society had already left
stops.campa: On the Theory of Compound Colours, and the Relations of the Colours of the Spectrum goes before the Royal Society, and the Rumford Medal follows it. What it establishes is that human colour vision is three-dimensional because the eye is three-dimensional, not because light is. The evidence is the spinning tops and a long box he built himself, fitted with a slit, prisms and mirrors, at which an observer sits with one eye to the aperture and matches any colour of the spectrum against a mixture of three others until the two halves of the field agree.
suggested_refs: Maxwell's colour box, and the Rumford Medal of the Royal Society, 1860
sources: James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
Wikipedia, 'Royal Society'
Wikipedia, 'Burlington House'

stops.name: Glenlair, smallpox
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1860; the month and day are an estimate within that summer
stops.campa: At Glenlair he contracts smallpox and comes close to dying of it. Katherine nurses him through the fever in a house well out of reach of any town, and every account written afterwards credits her with saving his life. He carries the marks. While he is in that bed, Aberdeen is being reorganised: Marischal and King's are merging into one university, and there is to be one chair of natural philosophy where there had been two. The other holder of that title, David Thomson of King's College Aberdeen, has the seniority.
suggested_refs: Campbell and Garnett's account of the 1860 illness at Glenlair
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: King's College London, the chair on the Strand
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is attested to 1860; the month and day are set to the opening of the session as an estimate
stops.campa: Marischal and King's College Aberdeen are merged, one chair of natural philosophy survives where there were two, the senior man David Thomson keeps it, and Maxwell is out of a post at twenty-nine. King's College London appoints him to its own chair the same year, and the Royal Society elects him a Fellow the next. The five years that follow are the most productive of his life. The London load is heavy through all of them: laboratory instruction, examinations, evening classes for artisans after the working day.
suggested_refs: King's College London, Strand, natural philosophy department records 1860-1865
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org

stops.name: Royal Institution, the tartan ribbon
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 May 1861 by the Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology and Wikipedia; the verification pass could not re-check the date or Thomas Sutton's role against a primary source. The pin is the Royal Institution coordinate already carried in charles_babbage.journey.json
stops.campa: In the Albemarle Street theatre he sets three lanterns on one screen. Thomas Sutton has photographed a tartan ribbon three times over, through red, green and blue filters. Maxwell projects the three negatives back through matching filters, superposed on the one screen. It is the first demonstration that three separations and three filters are enough to rebuild any colour a human eye can see, and he is using it only to illustrate a lecture on vision. Above the heads of the audience in Albemarle Street, the ribbon comes up in colour.
suggested_refs: Thomas Sutton's three filtered negatives of the tartan ribbon, 1861, the first colour photograph by three-colour projection
sources: James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org

stops.name: King's College London, On Physical Lines of Force
stops.date_confidence: published in four parts across 1861 and 1862; the date is set to the start of 1862 to order the segment
stops.campa: He builds a machine out of nothing: space packed with spinning molecular vortices, and between them, so that neighbouring vortices can turn the same way, a layer of tiny idle wheels which are also the particles of electricity. He does not believe the model. It is scaffolding, put up in order to be taken down. Then he computes the speed at which a disturbance would travel through it, using a ratio of electrical units that had been measured on a laboratory bench for reasons having nothing to do with light, and the number that comes out is the speed of light.
stops.quote: light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena
stops.quote_source: James Clerk Maxwell, On Physical Lines of Force (1861-62), Wikisource transcription; the sentence opens 'We can scarcely avoid the inference that'
suggested_refs: Maxwell's plate of the vortex and idle-wheel model, On Physical Lines of Force, Part II
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Wikisource, 'On Physical Lines of Force'

stops.name: Burlington House, A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 December 1864. The venue is Burlington House; the Royal Society had left Somerset House in 1857, and sources placing this reading at Somerset House are in error
stops.campa: He reads the paper to the Royal Society and the vortices are gone. What is left is the field itself, treated as a dynamical system with energy stored in it, obeying twenty equations in twenty variables and containing one term nobody had needed before: the displacement current, a current in empty space where no charge moves. Out of that he derives a transverse wave travelling at the speed of light, and stops calling the agreement a coincidence. Light is an electromagnetic disturbance. The Philosophical Transactions print the paper the following year.
suggested_refs: Maxwell, 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1865)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
Wikipedia, 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field'

stops.name: King's College London, the chair given up
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor dates the departure to spring 1865; the month and day are an estimate. Maxwell was thirty-three at the time and turned thirty-four on 13 June that year, so accounts giving his age as thirty-four at the resignation are wrong
stops.campa: Five years into the London chair he resigns it. He is thirty-three, in the middle of the work on the field, and he goes home to Galloway to be a laird. He keeps the Royal Society, the electrical standards committee and the London examining, and travels down for them, but the daily teaching stops. From here on the physics is done in a country house with no colleague inside a day's journey. The reason he gives for going is that he wants time to write.
suggested_refs: The British Association committee on electrical standards, on which Maxwell continued to serve after 1865
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell

segments.name: Glenlair Again: The Demon and the Governor

stops.name: Glenlair, the branch and the erysipelas
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1865, soon after the return to Glenlair; the month and day are an estimate. The riding-injury detail comes from the Campbell and Garnett biography by way of secondary accounts and is not corroborated by any primary medical record
stops.campa: Riding on his own land he takes a branch to the head, and the wound turns to erysipelas, the skin infection that killed people as a matter of routine before antibiotics. He is dangerously ill for weeks. Katherine nurses him again, as she had through the smallpox five years earlier, and he recovers. He then extends the house, close to doubling it, and settles into the arrangement that holds for six years: mornings at the desk, afternoons on the estate, a swim in the river with the dog.
suggested_refs: The Glenlair extension of 1867, designed with Maxwell's own involvement
sources: Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), as summarized in secondary accounts
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Glenlair, the neat-fingered being
stops.date_confidence: the letter to Tait is attested to 1867; the month and day are an estimate within that year
stops.campa: Writing to Tait, he proposes a creature. Put a partition across a vessel of gas, with a small hole in it and a door on the hole, and station at the door a very observant and neat-fingered being who opens it for fast molecules going one way and slow ones going the other. No work is done. The gas separates itself into hot and cold. William Thomson will call the being a demon, over Maxwell's objection, and the name is the one that lasts. What the second law describes, Maxwell means to show, is not a property of matter but the limit of what a creature of ordinary size can find out about it.
suggested_refs: Maxwell to Peter Guthrie Tait, 1867, the letter first setting out the sorting being
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell', citing Maxwell's 1867 correspondence with Tait

stops.name: Glenlair, On Governors
stops.date_confidence: the paper is attested to 1868; the month and day are set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: He publishes a paper on the centrifugal governors that hold steam engines and telescope drives at a steady speed. It is short, dry and practical, a paper about a brass object with two spinning balls on it. He treats the whole regulating loop as one system of differential equations, and the roots of those equations decide whether a disturbance in the machine dies away or grows until the thing shakes itself apart. The conditions he writes down for those roots are what later engineers will use on machines that correct themselves.
suggested_refs: Maxwell, 'On Governors', Proceedings of the Royal Society (1868)
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Glenlair, Theory of Heat
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia gives 1871 for the publication of Theory of Heat and is followed here; the Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology places it inside a compressed 1870 entry bundling several years of items. Month and day set to 01
stops.campa: The textbook comes out: a short book on heat for students, written in plain sentences by a man who had spent fifteen years on the statistics of molecules and could therefore say what a temperature is without an equation on the first page. The sorting being appears in it publicly for the first time, in a chapter on the limits of the second law. Two years earlier the Royal Society of Edinburgh had given him its Keith Prize. He is forty and holds no chair anywhere.
suggested_refs: Maxwell, Theory of Heat (Longmans, 1871), chapter on the limitation of the second law
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org

segments.name: The Cavendish: A Laboratory Built From Nothing

stops.name: Cambridge, the chair that does not exist yet
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is attested to 1871; the month and day are an estimate. The pin is central Cambridge, the appointment not being tied to a building that existed at the time
stops.campa: William Cavendish, seventh Duke of Devonshire and Chancellor of the university, offers to pay for a chair of experimental physics and a building to hold it. Cambridge, which has taught mathematical physics for two centuries without letting an undergraduate touch an instrument, takes the money. Maxwell accepts the chair with some reluctance and on provisional terms, then designs the laboratory himself: the site, the benches, the ventilation, the gas and water runs, the specification of every instrument to be bought for it.
suggested_refs: The Duke of Devonshire's endowment of the Cavendish chair and laboratory, 1870-1871
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Wikipedia, 'Cavendish Laboratory'

stops.name: Cavendish Laboratory, A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism
stops.date_confidence: publication is attested to 1873; the month and day are set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: Two volumes, and much of it cast in the quaternion notation of William Rowan Hamilton, which Maxwell adopts because he wants a reader to think in directed quantities rather than in components. British readers find it close to impassable. Writing to R. B. Hayward in December 1892, William Thomson calls quaternions an unmixed evil to everyone who touched them, naming Clerk Maxwell among the injured. Continental physicists and one telegraph engineer will spend a generation boiling the notation down to the four equations that get taught afterwards. The physics inside the book is correct as it stands.
suggested_refs: Maxwell, A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, 2 vols. (Clarendon Press, 1873)
William Thomson to R. B. Hayward, December 1892, quoted in Silvanus P. Thompson, Life of William Thomson (1910)
sources: James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Cambridge, the Eranus essay on free will
stops.date_confidence: attested to 11 February 1873, read to the Eranus club at Cambridge; the meeting place within Cambridge is not established and the pin is central Cambridge
stops.campa: To a small Cambridge club he reads an essay asking whether physics, as it advances, favours determinism or leaves room for the freedom of the will. His answer is careful and satisfies neither party. Determinism holds well enough for stable systems, but there are singular points at which a system's whole future turns on a quantity too small to be measured, and at those points the calculation gives out. He does not claim that this rescues the freedom of the will. Whether anything does, he leaves open. The essay is read once, to the club, and not printed until after his death.
stops.quote: No leopard can change his spots, nor can any one by merely wishing it, or, as some say, willing it, introduce discontinuity into his course of existence. Our free will at the best is like that of Lucretius's atoms,—which at quite uncertain times and places deviate in an uncertain manner from their course.
stops.quote_source: James Clerk Maxwell, essay read to the Eranus club, Cambridge, 11 February 1873, printed entire in Campbell and Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.441
suggested_refs: Maxwell's Eranus essay on determinism and the freedom of the will, Campbell and Garnett (1882), p.441
sources: Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.441

stops.name: Cavendish Laboratory, the doors open
stops.date_confidence: attested to 16 June 1874
stops.campa: The building on Free School Lane is finished and opens. It has workshops, a lecture theatre, rooms sited away from iron for magnetic work, and benches Maxwell specified himself. The whole cost, building and apparatus together, has come out of the Duke of Devonshire's own pocket. Cambridge now has a place where a student can measure something rather than write about it. The Tripos rewards paper and the laboratory is optional, so in the first years hardly anyone comes. Maxwell spends his afternoons in the building, alone, adjusting instruments.
suggested_refs: The Cavendish Laboratory, Free School Lane, New Museums Site, Cambridge, opened 16 June 1874
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'Cavendish Laboratory'

stops.name: Cavendish Laboratory, the Cavendish papers
stops.date_confidence: the editorial work is attested to have begun in 1874 and the edition appeared in 1879; the month and day are an estimate
stops.campa: The Duke hands him a box of manuscripts: Henry Cavendish's unpublished electrical work, written a century earlier by a man so withdrawn that he left instructions to his housekeeper in writing and published almost nothing. Colleagues think the labour a waste of the best mind in England. Maxwell gives five of his last years to it, deciphers the hand, repeats the experiments on the bench with his own apparatus, and shows that Cavendish had the inverse square law before Coulomb and the idea of potential before anyone. The Electrical Researches appears in 1879.
stops.quote: The lip of truth shall be established for ever.
stops.quote_source: Proverbs 12:19, the text Maxwell kept hung in his private room, noted by F. J. A. Hort in Campbell and Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.419
suggested_refs: The Electrical Researches of the Honourable Henry Cavendish, F.R.S., edited by James Clerk Maxwell (Cambridge University Press, 1879)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'Cavendish Laboratory'
Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.419

stops.name: Cambridge, the Rede Lecture on the telephone
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1878 by the Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, which also records the Volta Medal that year; the traditional Rede Lecture venue is the Senate House but this is unconfirmed, so the pin is central Cambridge. Month and day set to 01
stops.campa: He gives the university's Rede Lecture on a device two years old, explaining the telephone to an audience most of whom have never seen one. The instrument turns speech into a varying current and the current back into speech, which is to say it runs on the electromagnetism he spent his life on, shrunk into a box a man holds against his ear. The waves his own equations demand, the free ones travelling through empty space at the speed of light, have still not been made in any laboratory on earth.
suggested_refs: The Rede Lecture, Cambridge, 1878, on the telephone
sources: James Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology, clerkmaxwellfoundation.org
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell

stops.name: Cambridge, the last lecture course
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1879; the day is set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: He finishes his lecture course in May with the pain in his abdomen already constant. He is forty-seven and has been ill for months without saying so to anyone. In the same weeks he is trying to review W. K. Clifford's Lectures and Essays, a book whose materialism he intends to answer, and he tells Hort exactly where the trouble lies: the argument needs demolishing and the author was a friend. The review never gets written. He goes north to Glenlair for the summer.
stops.quote: there were many things in the book that wanted trouncing, and yet the trouncing had to be done with extreme care and gentleness, Clifford was such a nice fellow.
stops.quote_source: Maxwell's own words during his last illness, recorded by Professor F. J. A. Hort in a letter to Lewis Campbell of 4 February 1882, printed in Campbell and Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.420
suggested_refs: W. K. Clifford, Lectures and Essays (1879), the book Maxwell meant to review
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.420

stops.name: Glenlair, the physician's letter
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 October 1879, the date of Dr Lorraine's letter to Dr Paget
stops.campa: The summer at Glenlair does not work. He grows thinner week by week and cannot eat. The doctor from Castle Douglas, J. W. Lorraine, is called out to the house, examines him, and writes to Cambridge reporting both what he has found and what he thinks of the man he found it in. The disease is the one that killed his mother, in the same part of the body. He is forty-eight. There is nothing at Glenlair that can help him. He asks to be taken back to Cambridge.
stops.quote: he is one of the best men I have ever met, and a greater merit than his scientific attainments is his being, so far as human judgment can discern, a most perfect example of a Christian gentleman.
stops.quote_source: Dr J. W. Lorraine of Castle Douglas to Dr Paget, 5 October 1879, printed in Campbell and Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.412
suggested_refs: Dr Lorraine's letter of 5 October 1879, Campbell and Garnett (1882), p.412
sources: Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.412
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Cambridge, the return
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 October 1879
stops.campa: He and Katherine come back to Cambridge on the eighth of October. He can scarcely walk. The Cambridge physicians confirm what Lorraine found in Galloway and give him about a month, and he takes the sentence without visible disturbance and goes on making arrangements: for Katherine, for the laboratory, for the papers. His parish priest, W. H. Guillemard, attends him through the weeks that follow and is asked, visit after visit, to read the burial service aloud at the bedside.
stops.quote: My dear friend, you have been a true under shepherd to me: read me, before you go, the beautiful prayer out of the Burial Service, 'Suffer me not at my last hour.'
stops.quote_source: Maxwell to the Rev. Dr W. H. Guillemard, recalled in Guillemard's letter of 9 December 1879 to the Rev. Isaac Bowman, printed in Campbell and Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), pp.415-416
suggested_refs: Guillemard's letter of 9 December 1879 on Maxwell's last weeks
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), pp.415-416

stops.name: Cambridge, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 November 1879; the sources gathered do not name the house or street where he died, so the pin is central Cambridge
stops.campa: He dies on the fifth of November, forty-eight years old, of the abdominal cancer commonly reported as of the stomach. His cousin Colin Mackenzie is in the room, and Mackenzie is the one who writes down afterwards what was said in it. A few minutes before the end, held up in the bed and struggling for breath, Maxwell says slowly and distinctly: God help me! God help my wife! Then he says, Colin, you are strong, lift me up. A little after that he asks to be laid down lower again, and makes the last of his puns on the word low.
stops.quote: Lay me down lower, for I am very low myself, and it suits me to lie low.
stops.quote_source: Maxwell's words at the last, recorded by his cousin Colin Mackenzie, who was present; Campbell and Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.416
suggested_refs: Colin Mackenzie's eyewitness account of 5 November 1879, Campbell and Garnett (1882), p.416
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'
Lewis Campbell and William Garnett, The Life of James Clerk Maxwell (1882), p.416

stops.name: Parton Kirk, the burial
stops.date_confidence: the burial is attested to November 1879; the day is not established in the sources gathered and is set here only to order the segment after the death
stops.campa: The body is carried north to Galloway and buried inside the ruined walls of the old kirk at Parton, in the burial ground near Castle Douglas, a few miles from Glenlair. His father lies in the same yard. Katherine will be laid in the same plot seven years later, in 1886. Which day in November the coffin went into the ground is not recorded in anything reached. There is no state funeral and no grave among the kings in the Abbey. He goes into the ground of the parish his family has held land in for generations, under a small stone.
suggested_refs: The Maxwell family plot within the ruins of the Old Kirk, Parton burial ground, Dumfries and Galloway

segments.name: The Grave, the Ruin, and the Name

stops.name: Cavendish Laboratory, the papers put in order
stops.date_confidence: posthumous. Niven's two-volume Scientific Papers appeared in 1890 and the month and day are set to 01; the second edition of the Treatise was completed by Niven in 1881 and a third prepared by J. J. Thomson in 1892
stops.campa: The Treatise had been left unrevised at his death. William Davidson Niven finishes the second edition in 1881, J. J. Thomson prepares a third in 1892, and in 1890 Niven brings out the two volumes of the Scientific Papers, everything Maxwell published, gathered for the first time in one place. That edition settles how the next hundred years read him. A century after his death P. M. Harman begins a three-volume scholarly edition of the letters and papers and finishes it in 2002.
suggested_refs: W. D. Niven, ed., The Scientific Papers of James Clerk Maxwell, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1890)
P. M. Harman, ed., The Scientific Letters and Papers of James Clerk Maxwell, 3 vols. (1990, 1995, 2002)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of James Clerk Maxwell, bibliography
Wikipedia, 'A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism'
Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell'

stops.name: Glenlair, the house burns
stops.date_confidence: posthumous. The fire is attested to 1929 by Wikipedia's article on Glenlair; the month and day are set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: Fifty years after his death the house he had extended to his own plans catches fire and is gutted. The roof goes, the floors go, and the rooms where the Treatise was written stand open to the sky. What is left is a shell in a field in Kirkcudbrightshire, and no one lives in it again. A trust will later work to stabilise the walls so that they at least stay standing, and the shell is what the photographs show. The record gives the year, 1929, and does not say what started the fire.
suggested_refs: The Maxwell at Glenlair Trust and its work stabilising the ruin
sources: Wikipedia, 'Glenlair House'
Wikipedia, 'Glenlair'

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the memorial stone
stops.date_confidence: posthumous, attested to 30 September 1931; the stone was replaced by a cast-iron version in 1976. The pin is the Westminster Abbey coordinate already carried in newton.journey.json
stops.campa: On the centenary of his birth a memorial stone is set into the Abbey nave, north of Newton's grave, and another laid beside it for Michael Faraday, whose lines of force he had turned into mathematics seventy-five years earlier. The Latin says only that this is the memory of James Clerk Maxwell, 1831 to 1879. He is buried in Galloway, and the stone says so. By this date the maxwell is a unit of magnetic flux, recommended at the Paris congress of 1900 and confirmed unanimously at Oslo in 1930.
suggested_refs: The Maxwell and Faraday memorial stones in the nave of Westminster Abbey, unveiled 30 September 1931
James Clerk Maxwell: A Commemorative Volume, 1831-1931 (Cambridge University Press, 1931)

stops.name: 14 India Street, the birthplace bought back
stops.date_confidence: posthumous. The James Clerk Maxwell Foundation was established by Sydney Ross in 1977 and acquired 14 India Street in 1993; the month and day are set to 01 as unknown
stops.campa: The house he was born in and left at two years old is bought by a foundation set up in his name and refurbished as a small museum and library. Sydney Ross, a chemist, founded the trust in 1977, and it took sixteen years to get the house. He never lived there as an adult, and of the buildings of his life it is the one still standing whole. It holds family material, instruments, and the chronology against which everything else printed about him is checked.
suggested_refs: The James Clerk Maxwell Foundation museum and library, 14 India Street, Edinburgh
sources: Wikipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell Foundation'

stops.name: George Street, Edinburgh, the statue
stops.date_confidence: posthumous, attested to 25 November 2008 by the Clerk Maxwell Foundation chronology. The coordinate is the eastern end of George Street near St Andrew Square and is an estimate; two earlier working values for this statue, 55.9548 -3.1936 and 55.9548 -3.1966, both fall well north of the street and are rejected
stops.campa: Alexander Stoddart's bronze goes up at the east end of George Street, a few streets from the house he was born in. The unveiling comes a hundred and twenty-nine years after his death, in a city that had let his name go quiet outside the universities. Inside physics it had never gone quiet. The bronze shows him seated, the colour top in his hand, his dog Toby lying at his feet. Of everything he did, the object the sculptor put in his hand is the painted disc he spun in Aberdeen to make the eye report a number.
suggested_refs: Alexander Stoddart's bronze of James Clerk Maxwell, east end of George Street, Edinburgh, unveiled 25 November 2008
